tickets.title: "Internal site loads by IP, but not by name"
tickets.summary: Users can reach 'http://172.18.2.50' but get a 404/Not Found when they type 'http://portal.local'.

triage.q: If the IP works but the name doesn't, which system is failing?

diagnosis.q: What is missing in the DNS Forward Lookup Zone?

fix.q: How do you fix the translation?

debrief.summary: DNS is the 'translator' for the network.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You used the 'IP vs Name' test to prove the website was actually healthy. This proved the problem was just a 'language' issue. Adding the A-record gave the computers the map they needed to turn the human-friendly name into the server's real address.

tickets.title: "Google and external sites aren't resolving"
tickets.summary: Internal file shares and local sites work, but no one in the office can reach any website on the internet.

triage.q: Where does your DNS server look if it doesn't know the answer to a name?

options: The server doesn't have 'Forwarders' configured to ask the internet for help
Add a Public DNS (like 8.8.8.8) to the 'Forwarders' tab

debrief.summary: Forwarders bridge the gap between private and public networks.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You identified that your server was an expert on your office, but 'blind' to the world. By adding a Forwarder, you gave your server a 'lifeline' to call whenever a user asks for an external site it doesn't recognize.

tickets.title: "Security log shows an IP, but I need the hostname"
tickets.summary: The firewall log says 10.0.0.45 is downloading huge files. You need to find out which computer that is using `nslookup 10.0.0.45`.

triage.q: Which zone type handles turning an IP into a Name?

options: There is no 'PTR' record created for that subnet

fix.q: How do you enable this feature?
options: Create a Reverse Lookup Zone for the subnet

debrief.summary: Reverse Lookups provide 'Caller ID' for your network.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You realized that DNS is usually a one-way street (Name to IP). By creating the Reverse Zone, you enabled 'PTR' records, which act like a reverse-phonebook, letting you track down mystery devices based on their IP address alone.

tickets.title: "Server move resulted in intermittent connection errors"
tickets.summary: A server moved to 10.0.0.50, but DNS still shows the old 10.0.0.20 address. Half the users can't connect.

triage.q: What happens if a name has two 'A' records with different IPs?
options: It uses 'Round Robin' and switches between them

diagnosis.q: Why is the old record still there?
options: The record is 'stale' because Scavenging isn't cleaning up old entries
Manually delete the old record and enable 'Scavenging'

debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You found a 'ghost' in the machine. Because DNS didn't 'forget' the old IP, it was sending half your users to a dead address. Deleting it and setting up Scavenging ensures the phonebook stays accurate by automatically removing old, unused entries.

tickets.title: "Marketing wants 'shop.local' to point to our web server"
tickets.summary: The web server's real name is `web-cluster-01`. Marketing wants a shorter, prettier name for the users.

triage.q: Which record type creates an 'Alias' or nickname?

diagnosis.q: Why use an Alias instead of another A-Record?
options: If the server's IP changes, you only update one A-Record and the Alias stays linked

debrief.summary: CNAMEs allow servers to have multiple 'identities'.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You gave the server a nickname. This is best practice because it separates the 'technical' name from the 'marketing' name. If you ever replace the server hardware, you just point the nickname to the new machine and the users never even notice.

tickets.title: "We can't receive any outside emails"
tickets.summary: Internal email works, and you can send out, but no external mail is reaching your company domain.

triage.q: Which record tells the world where your mail server is?

options: The internet's DNS doesn't know which server is the 'Mailbox' for your domain
Add an MX record pointing to your mail server

debrief.summary: MX records are the 'mailing address' for your domain.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You identified that the world knew your server existed, but didn't know it was a 'Mail' server. The MX record acts like a sign on the building that says 'Deliver Mail Here,' ensuring the internet's postmen know where to drop the letters.

tickets.title: "Logins are taking 5 minutes to complete"
tickets.summary: Workstations can ping the Domain Controller, but they take forever to 'find' it during the login screen.

triage.q: Which record type helps a PC 'locate' services like Active Directory?

options: The PC is 'hunting' for a DC because the Service map (SRV records) is missing

fix.q: How do you re-register these records?
options: Restart the 'Netlogon' service on the Domain Controller

debrief.summary: SRV records are the 'GPS' for Windows services.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You realized that just 'knowing the name' isn't enough; the PC needs to know which server is the 'Login Expert.' Restarting Netlogon forces the DC to announce itself and repopulate those GPS coordinates (SRV records) in DNS.

tickets.title: "Changes on DC-01 aren't showing up on DC-02"
tickets.summary: You added a record to your primary DNS server, but your backup server still has no record of it after two hours.
artifact: Zone Properties: 'Allow Zone Transfers' is unchecked.

triage.q: How does a backup DNS server get its info from the primary?

options: The primary server is 'guarding' the data and won't let the backup download it
Enable 'Allow Zone Transfers' to the secondary server

debrief.summary: Zone Transfers are the 'sync' engine of DNS.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You identified a security gate. DNS servers don't just share their data with anyone. By enabling Zone Transfers, you 'unlocked' the database for DC-02, ensuring your backup server stays just as smart as your primary one.

tickets.title: "Pinging a deleted server still returns an IP"
tickets.summary: You deleted a server's DNS record, but when you ping it from your desk, it still somehow 'finds' the old IP.

triage.q: Where does a computer 'remember' old DNS answers locally?

diagnosis.q: Why is your PC still seeing a deleted record?
options: The PC is using its local cache instead of asking the server

fix.q: How do you 'empty' the PC's memory?

debrief.summary: Local cache can hide the truth of a fix.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You learned that the 'server' isn't the only one with a memory. Your PC was trying to be 'fast' by using an old answer it already had saved. Flushing the DNS forced the PC to look at the real, updated phonebook on the server.

tickets.title: "External resolution died when Google DNS went down"
tickets.summary: You use 8.8.8.8 as your forwarder. When it went offline, your whole office lost internet browsing.
artifact: Setting: 'Use root hints if no forwarders available' is UNCHECKED.

options: The 13 'Master' DNS servers for the whole internet
The server wasn't allowed to use its 'emergency backup' (Root Hints) when the forwarder failed

fix.q: How do you enable the fail-safe?
options: Check the box to 'Use root hints if no forwarders are available'

debrief.summary: Root Hints are the 'Last Resort' for internet resolution.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You found the safety net. Forwarders are like calling a 'smart friend,' but Root Hints are like 'looking it up in the library yourself.' Enabling this ensures the office can still browse even if your primary forwarders go offline.
